notes: Adapted from Purge explanations.json (key/display_name/tag/explanation/aliases/kind, no paths). Windows additions: tier, removal, preconditions, verified, verified_date, scanner_id. No mode field: there are no modes. Never-delete items never appear here. Paths come from scanners + the deletion safety policy, never from this file.

entries.explanation: Temporary files Windows and your apps left behind. Only files older than a day are offered, so files an app is using right now stay put. Apps recreate what they need.

Cached web pages, images and scripts from your browsers. Only cache leaves are touched; history, passwords, bookmarks and signed-in sessions stay untouched. Pages may load a little slower the first time after clearing.
Caches from chat apps, editors, launchers and streaming apps. Only cache leaves are touched; settings, chats, projects and downloads stay untouched. Close the app first so nothing is in use.

Downloaded packages and build outputs from your dev tools. Your tools re-download and rebuild them, so the next build is slower and needs the network. Your projects, settings and credentials are untouched. Package stores other projects link into are never touched by hand.

Compiled shaders your graphics drivers and games built. They rebuild automatically, but games may stutter the first time they run after clearing while shaders recompile. Not something to clear routinely.

Quick Boot snapshots and the scratch cache image of your Android virtual devices. User data, SD card images, settings and the debug keystore are never included. The emulator recreates snapshots as needed.
Crash dumps and error reports Windows and your apps already recorded. Clearing them removes diagnostic records you would only need when reporting a bug; it does not affect the apps themselves.

The thumbnail and icon databases File Explorer uses to show previews. Only the database files themselves are removed, never the folder. Explorer rebuilds previews as you browse, so folders may show generic icons briefly.

Downloaded updates, the Delivery Optimization cache, the Windows temp folder and system crash dumps. Needs administrator rights, because Windows locks these locations. Never clear downloaded updates while an update is in progress.

Sizes only. Servicing logs, diagnostic traces, event logs, the font cache and the Search index can only be cleared safely through Windows or their own tools, so Purge for Windows reports them and tells you where to act. Never delete these files by hand.

Windows setup logs, web server logs and Performance Monitor reports. Setup logs are the only record if an upgrade failed, so only clear them once Windows is running well. Performance Monitor reports are your own recordings — check them first.

Installer files sitting loose in Downloads, older than a week. They may be the only copy of that version of an app — if you still need to reinstall it, keep it. Only loose files in Downloads itself are listed; programs inside folders are left alone.

Large files in Downloads untouched for at least 30 days. They are your files, not cache — they may be the only copy. Pick the ones you no longer want; everything goes to the Recycle Bin, so you can put them back.

Outlook's offline copies of your mailbox (.ost files). They rebuild from the server, but mail kept only on this PC does not come back — check the Outbox for unsent mail and export any 'This computer only' folders first. .pst files are never listed: they may be the only copy of the mail.
Photos, videos and files received in WhatsApp. They may be the only copy on this PC, so check inside WhatsApp before deleting. Messages and chats themselves are never included.
Clips and screenshots recorded with Game Bar. They are your videos and pictures, not cache — pick the ones you no longer want. Only loose .mp4 and .png files in the Captures folder are listed.

Large Steam games you have not played in 60 days. Removal goes through Steam's own uninstaller, which is permanent — it is not moved to the Recycle Bin. Check that your saves are in Steam Cloud before removing a game.

Sizes only. Virtual disks never shrink on their own, but Purge for Windows never deletes them — a wrong delete destroys the whole machine. Compact or remove each one through its own tool; use the folder button to open it.

The previous Windows installation and upgrade staging folders. Only Windows itself can remove these safely, so this opens Settings. Only clear them once Windows is running well after the upgrade — until then, they are your way back.

What is currently in the Recycle Bin. Purge for Windows never empties the bin — emptying it is permanent, and it is Windows' job. Open the bin in File Explorer to restore or permanently delete what is inside.
Legacy web cache from Internet Explorer-era components. Modern browsers do not use it. Cookies and the WebCache database are left alone: cookies sign you out, and the database holds history.

Cache leaves (Cache, Code Cache, GPUCache, shader caches) from Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi and Chromium. Profiles, history, cookies and logins are never touched. Service Worker storage is never touched: it holds offline web-app data.
Firefox's HTTP cache and shader caches in the Local profile. Site storage in the Roaming profile holds real web-app data and is never included.
Opera's cache leaves. The profile itself (Roaming) is never touched; since Opera 100.x the cache may live under the Roaming profile's Default folder, so those exact leaves are probed too.
Chromium cache leaves from Electron apps (chat, editors, AI assistants). Only validated cache leaves are touched — never Service Worker or IndexedDB storage, which hold app data.

Spotify's streaming cache and built-in browser cache. Offline downloads (Storage) are left alone — clearing them would delete music you downloaded for offline listening. In-app clearing is preferred when available.

Web caches from game launchers (Battle.net, EA App, GOG Galaxy, Ubisoft Connect, Epic). Contents only, launcher closed. Games, saves and sign-ins live elsewhere and are never touched. Xbox has no hand-delete folder, so it stays out.

VS Code's web caches, per-version bytecode, cached extension packages and logs. Settings, workspace state and chat history live elsewhere and are never included. VS Code Insiders is covered the same way.
Adobe's shared media cache: conformed audio, waveforms and indexes. Projects, footage and presets live elsewhere. Adobe rebuilds the cache on next open, so the first open afterwards is slower.
Zoom's data and logs folders — the documented clear. Settings and local recordings live elsewhere and are never included.
Signal's logs only. Messages and attachments live only on this PC and are end-to-end encrypted — the rest of the folder is never touched.
Outlook's roaming settings cache. It rebuilds itself and holds no mail; the mailbox files themselves are a separate, check-first category.

New Teams' WebView2 cache leaves, logs and cached avatars. Settings and sign-in live elsewhere. Microsoft warns not to clear Teams data to fix missing messages — use Teams' own Reset for that instead.
DirectX shader cache. Sources disagree on the exact location, so both reported spots are probed. Shaders rebuild on next run; games may stutter briefly while they recompile.
NVIDIA's DirectX, OpenGL and compute shader caches. Contents only. Drivers rebuild them; games may stutter briefly the first time they run afterwards.
AMD's DirectX, Vulkan and OpenGL shader caches. Paths are community-reported rather than vendor-documented. Drivers rebuild them; games may stutter briefly the first time they run afterwards.

Intel's shader cache. The location is reported rather than vendor-documented, so it is probed and only offered when it actually exists. Drivers rebuild it; games may stutter briefly the first time they run afterwards.
Precompiled shaders Steam downloaded for your games. They re-download or rebuild as needed; games may stutter briefly the first time they run afterwards. Game files and saves are never touched.
Steam's encrypted download chunks. They re-download if a download resumes; in-progress and paused downloads live elsewhere and are left alone.
One virtual device's Quick Boot snapshots and scratch cache image. User data, SD card images, config and the debug keystore are never included.
Crash dumps Windows collected from your apps. They are diagnostic records only; clearing them does not affect the apps.
Windows Error Reporting archives and queues (contents only). Diagnostic records you would only need when reporting a bug to Microsoft.

Browser crash uploads: already-sent or uploadable copies from Chromium browsers. The report IDs stay listed in each browser's own crash page. Unsent reports in the pending folder go with the rest — they are diagnostic data, not your files.
The thumbnail and icon database files themselves. Explorer rebuilds them as you browse.

Update packages Windows already downloaded. Clearing them means Windows re-downloads an update if it still needs it. Never clear while an update is in progress, and never touch the rest of the update store by hand.
Update chunks Windows cached to share with other PCs on your network. Clearing them only costs re-downloads. Needs administrator rights.
The system temp folder's contents (the folder itself stays). Only files older than a day are offered. Needs administrator rights.

Minidumps, the full memory dump and live-kernel reports from system crashes. Diagnostic records only — but they can be the only trace of why the PC crashed, so keep them if you are troubleshooting a crash. Needs administrator rights.
Sizes only. Component servicing and DISM logs. Stop the Windows Modules Installer service first, then delete the contents. Never during an update.
Sizes only. Diagnostic trace logs. Delete in Settings, Privacy & security, Diagnostics & feedback, Delete diagnostic data.
Sizes only. Windows event logs. Clear in Event Viewer, keeping the Security log. Clearing cannot be undone.
Sizes only. Repair-only: only clear if fonts look broken, after stopping the Font Cache service. Never delete the cache file while the service is running.
Sizes only. Never delete the index file by hand. Rebuild in Indexing Options, Advanced, Rebuild — search will be slower until the rebuild finishes.

Setup logs from Windows installation and upgrades. They are the only record if an upgrade failed, so only clear them once Windows is running well. The copy under the previous-installation folders stays with that category, so the same bytes are never counted twice.
Web server logs older than 30 days. Only present when IIS is installed. Logs newer than 30 days stay, so recent traffic is still reviewable.
Your own Performance Monitor reports. They are your recordings, not cache — check them first. Only the contents are offered, never the folder itself.

Downloaded Maven artifacts. Your builds re-download them, so the next build is slower and needs the network. No owner clean command exists for the repository itself, so the cache is recycled and can be put back.
Gradle's caches and wrapper distributions. Gradle re-downloads them on the next build. The Gradle daemon is stopped first so nothing holds the files open.
Cargo's registry cache, sources and git checkouts. Cargo re-downloads them on the next build. Installed tools and credentials are never touched.

Go's build cache and module cache, resolved with go env so custom locations are found too. Go's own clean command is the vendor-correct way to clear them and deletes permanently, so it only ever runs with your explicit confirmation; otherwise the cache is recycled and can be put back. Read-only files in the module cache are why hand-deletion needs care.

NuGet's global packages folder. Packages restore on the next build, so the next build is slower and needs the network. The config file with registry credentials is never touched. The owner command (dotnet nuget locals --clear) is the vendor way; the Recycle Bin route can be put back.
C/C++ IntelliSense indexes for VS Code. Clearing them forces a full re-index of every C/C++ project, so this stays your call.

npm's download cache, npx cache and logs. The location is resolved with npm itself, so custom configurations are found too; documented defaults are probed as well. Packages re-download on the next install.
pip's download cache. Packages re-download on the next install. Installed packages and virtual environments are never touched.
Yarn's download cache. Packages re-download on the next install. Project folders are never touched.
NuGet's HTTP cache and plugin cache. The global packages folder is a separate, check-first item; the config file with registry credentials is never touched.
Chocolatey's HTTP cache, cleared the documented manual way. Installed packages are never touched.
WhatsApp's local media copies (photos, videos, files). They may be the only copy on this PC, so check inside WhatsApp before deleting. Messages and chats live elsewhere and are never included.

One mailbox's offline copy. It rebuilds from the server, but mail kept only on this PC does not come back — check the Outbox for unsent mail and export any 'This computer only' folders first. Safer first steps: Compact Now in Outlook, or download less mail.
One Game Bar recording or screenshot. Your video or picture, not cache — pick the ones you no longer want. Everything goes to the Recycle Bin, so you can put them back.

Sizes only. VirtualBox, VMware and Hyper-V disks. Never delete a disk file by hand — snapshot chains and differencing disks break in ways that destroy the machine. Compact or remove through the virtualization tool.
Sizes only. WSL2 distribution disks. Compact with wsl --manage --compact while the distro is stopped; never delete the disk file by hand. Sparse mode is not recommended.
Sizes only. Prune unused images and build cache inside Docker first, then compact this disk. Never delete the file itself. Volumes are never auto-removed.
Sizes only. BlueStacks, LDPlayer, Nox and MEmu engine disks. Never delete a disk image by hand — the emulator breaks. Manage storage inside the emulator.

The hibernation file holds your PC's memory image for hibernation and fast startup. It is never deleted directly — only powercfg may remove it, by turning hibernation off. Turning hibernation off also disables fast startup.

Restore points let Windows roll back after a bad driver or update. Removing them is permanent and removes your way back — only ever through System Protection in Settings, never by hand. Keep at least the most recent one.
Stuck Background Intelligent Transfer jobs (Windows Update and app downloads). Only the BITS admin tool may cancel them — the queue database files must never be deleted by hand.
Setup and update diagnostic logs beyond the Panther folder. Only logs older than 30 days, and never while an update is in progress — they are the record of what an update did.

Upgrade staging folders left after a Windows upgrade. Only once the upgrade has completed and Windows is running well — until then they are part of the upgrade. Removal goes through Settings with the previous-installation category.

Repair-only. The notification database is only reset when notifications are actually broken, with the notification service stopped first. Routine clearing gains nothing and loses notification history.
Recent-item and Jump List records. Clearing them resets pinned items too, so pinned apps and files lose their shortcuts. Only clear when you actually want that reset.
Windows activity history (Timeline records). Only ever cleared through Settings — the history database must never be deleted by hand, or Timeline breaks.
The Windows Firewall log file. Only the log file itself is removed, at its resolved location. Needs administrator rights.
Stuck print-job files, only when the print queue is empty and the files are older than 7 days. Clearing them while a job is printing would lose the job.
BranchCache content cached for other PCs on the network. Only the netsh command may clear it — the cache files must never be deleted by hand.
ClickOnce application cache. Only the ClickOnce cache tool (dfshim) may clear it — the cache folders must never be deleted by hand, or ClickOnce apps break.
ASP.NET compilation output. Only with IIS stopped — clearing while a site is running breaks it. Sites recompile on next request, so the first request afterwards is slower.
Phone Link's local cache only. LocalState holds sign-in and device state and is never touched by hand.

Caches from Firefox-based browsers, found through each browser's profiles list rather than guessed folder names. Only cache leaves are touched; site storage is never included. Browsers without a profiles list are not offered.

Cache leaves from Electron apps not listed individually, found only where the app folder carries an Electron marker. Only validated cache leaves are touched — never Service Worker or IndexedDB storage.
Old Roblox client versions, keeping the newest one. Roblox updates by installing a new version folder and leaving the old ones behind.
Minecraft's logs only. Saves, mods, resource packs and installed versions are never touched — they are your game, not cache.
Conan's package cache, cleared with Conan's own cache command (vendor-documented). Packages re-download on the next build.
Detection-only for now: Unreal and Unity global cache locations still need live verification before anything is offered for cleaning. Nothing is deleted.
NVIDIA's compute shader cache, contents only. Drivers rebuild it as needed.
Detection-only for now: Autodesk and other creative-app cache locations still need verification before anything is offered for cleaning. Nothing is deleted.
Dropbox's hidden cache folder, found through Dropbox's own location file. Only with Dropbox quit and everything synced — clearing while files are still uploading would lose the uploads.

Sizes only, and no deletion ever. iPhone and iPad backups are the only copy of the device's data for many people. Manage them in iTunes or Apple Devices — Purge for Windows only reports how much space they take.
Hyper-V virtual disks compacted with Optimize-VHD. Only while the VM is off with no checkpoints, and only dynamic or differencing disks. Fixed disks and disks in a snapshot chain are never touched.

WSL disk files whose distribution is no longer registered, older than 30 days. The registration check must pass first — a registered distro's disk is its whole filesystem. Gated until the check is verified live.

Driver installer staging folders left by the PC manufacturer. Gated: a rename test and a driver backup come first, and folders marked as recovery data hide the whole category. The C:\DRIVERS location is disputed and stays out.
Repair handoffs only: when Search or Start is broken, Windows' own troubleshooters and the index rebuild are the fix. The index files themselves are never deleted by hand.
Handoffs only: Store apps are reset or repaired through Settings. Their LocalState folders are never deleted by hand — they hold sign-in and app state.
Podman, Rancher Desktop, minikube and kind disks and caches, queried through each tool. Paths are unverified, so nothing is offered until the tool queries are verified live.
AMD driver installer extracts. A rename test comes first: if the driver still works with the folder renamed, it is safe to remove. Intel installer extracts stay out — their location is unverified.

Groundwork only — the registry module is a later wave. When it arrives: allowlist-only classes (uninstall entries, App Paths, Run values, app keys, startup approvals), a restore point plus a verified export of every key before any change, and protected hives checked first. No heuristic sweeping, ever.
The Microsoft Store cache, cleared with wsreset — Windows' own tool for it. The Store rebuilds the cache on next open. Clearing is permanent (no Recycle Bin), so it needs confirmation.
Left alone on purpose. Windows manages Prefetch itself, and clearing it does not help — Windows just rebuilds it, and startup is slower until it does. No action is offered.
Windows Defender scan history, cleared through Windows Security. Quarantined items are never touched — they are isolated threats, not clutter.
Compact a WSL2 distro disk with wsl --manage --compact while the distro is stopped. Sparse mode is not recommended and is never suggested. The disk file itself is never deleted by hand.
Prune unused Docker images and build cache inside Docker. Volumes are never auto-removed — they hold container data that may be the only copy.
